Maladaptive Strategies.value: I detach myself from the memories
become overly compliant when feeling threatened
try hard not think about the trauma

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I remember the event I feel intense rage

Negative Appraisals.value: You can never know who will harm you
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a male torture survivor, sexual-trauma-specific verbal cues are possible only if sexual torture or sexual humiliation is part of the trauma, but the rest of the profile provides no corresponding sexual content in memory, appraisals, threat, or coping. As selected, this trigger appears disconnected from the trauma representation and is hard to justify clinically.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: The appraisal that others can visibly see what happened to him implies shame/marked visible contamination or exposure. That could occur after torture, but here it is not supported by the memory items, trigger content, or other appraisals, making it feel mismatched with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: Gambling as a coping strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is poorly linked to the active formulation. The main connected pattern is triggers ↔ negative appraisals with memory-linked re-experiencing and threat-driven compliance/detachment. Gambling introduces a separate excitement-seeking coping style that is not reflected elsewhere and feels clinically disconnected rather than integrated.

vignette: Mateo’s hands, mapped with decades of silvered scars from welding torches and grinding wheels, still carried the ghost of a different kind of binding. Forty years earlier, during the height of the political purges in his homeland, he had been dragged into a windowless concrete room where the heavy iron door sealed him inside. For three weeks, he had been stripped of every avenue of escape, his wrists secured to a cold pipe while rough hands used blunt objects against his ribs and thighs. The guards never spoke a coherent warning; they only measured his compliance with sudden strikes and the sharp, echoing reports of pistol fire fired against the wall to keep him kneeling. Those specific conditions—the absolute certainty that he could not move, the unrelenting physical violence, and the unpredictable reports of gunfire—had become etched into his nervous system. When they happened again in his present life, the past did not fade; it rushed forward to occupy the same air. The moment a compressor valve hissed or a metal clamp dropped with a metallic clang in his current shop, the crushing weight of that old room reasserted itself. Mateo would feel his chest tighten, certain that the same lack of options had returned, and that the sudden noise might be followed by another strike. That familiar dread quickly solidified into a hardened conviction: the world remained a place where anyone could decide to harm him, and nothing could prevent it. He carried a quiet, corrosive belief that he had been foolish in those cells, that his own choices had opened the door to such violence, and that he would never forgive himself for standing still while it happened. The sensory shock of the workshop did not just startle him; it pulled the memory of the room fully into the present, making his own ribs ache and his ears ring with phantom reports. Because the memory pressed forward with such visceral force, his tolerance for loud machinery or confined spaces plummeted, making him flinch at every dropped wrench or backfiring truck engine as proof that the cell had never truly closed. When the fear took hold, Mateo’s first instinct was not to flee or fight, but to fold. He would go still, lower his eyes, and agree to whatever the foreman or customer demanded, believing that quiet submission was the only safe route through danger. He forced himself to stop dwelling on the workshop sounds, deliberately pushing the images of the room out of his mind until the tension in his shoulders eased. Yet the very act of trying to silence his own thoughts made the suppressed material heavier. The fear that harm was always lurking just beyond the next corner taught him that his mind had to be locked down, that detaching from the memories was the only way to survive the day. His own body betrayed him in the present by treating every sudden noise as confirmation that the threat was still active. Over the years, the habits formed into a quiet erosion of his life. He stopped taking jobs that required working in tight machinery bays, and he withdrew from the local welding union gatherings where men gathered around loud grinders. The loss of his wife a few years prior had left him alone in a small apartment, where the silence felt safer until it suddenly felt threatening. He tried to explain what had happened to his daughter, but his voice would stutter, the narrative fracturing before he could find the end, which only deepened his isolation. What finally brought him to the clinic was not just the waking terrors or the way his hands trembled when a neighbor’s car backfired, but the realization that he was slowly closing off every room of his life. He came to the intake seeking a way to step out from under the weight of his own guilt and fear, hoping to find a space where he could stop waiting for the next shot, and where he might finally be allowed to remember without feeling like he was bleeding in real time.
